title: Heart, Great Vessels, and Pericardium
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter places the heart in the chest and works inward: its position and the chambers that form each surface, border, and radiographic contour; the front to back order of the chambers; the pericardium, its sinuses, and the nerve that carries its pain; the great vessels and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve; the internal features of each chamber; and the anatomy of blunt and penetrating chest trauma. Board questions rarely ask for a bare name. They describe a finding, such as hoarseness in mitral stenosis, shoulder pain in pericarditis, or hypotension with distended neck veins after a stab wound, and expect you to name the structure and explain the mechanism from position, embryology, and pressure in a closed space.
prerequisites: Surface landmarks of the thoracic wall and the divisions of the mediastinum at the sternal angle (T4 to T5 disc)
Heart tube looping, atrial septation, and the fate of the pharyngeal arch arteries (CV-1)
Histology of serous membranes and of the heart and vessel wall (CV-2)
Normal systemic and pulmonary pressures and the relation between pressure, volume, and compliance
The cervical plexus, the phrenic nerve, and the dermatomes of the neck and shoulder

connections.how: Looping of the heart tube explains why the right ventricle faces forward, and the sixth arch artery explains why the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch.
The SA node lies at the top of the crista terminalis and the right bundle branch runs in the moderator band, so internal chamber anatomy locates the conduction system.
The coronary arteries are the only branches of the ascending aorta and run in the grooves that mark the chamber boundaries described here.
Pericarditis, effusion, tamponade, and constriction are all explained by the layers, innervation, and stiffness of the pericardium.
Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, which then compresses the posterior structures described in this chapter.

sections.title: Position of the heart and the chambers that form its surfaces and borders

blocks.text: The transverse thoracic plane, through the sternal angle and the T4 to T5 disc, divides the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts, and the pericardium divides the inferior part into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments. The middle mediastinum holds the pericardium, the heart, and the roots of the great vessels. Behind it, the posterior mediastinum contains the esophagus and descending aorta, the neighbors that matter most for the posterior chamber.

The heart is rotated. Its base faces backward and to the right, its apex points forward, downward, and to the left, and about two thirds of it lies left of the median plane. Its right side faces forward, so the right ventricle, not the left, forms most of the front, the adult result of looping of the heart tube (CV-1).

On the chest wall, the outline runs from the left second costal cartilage to the right third cartilage (superior border), down to the right sixth cartilage just beside the sternum (right border), across to the left fifth intercostal space (inferior border), and back up to the left second cartilage (left border). The apex lies behind the left fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line, about 9 cm from the midline. Left ventricular contraction pushes it against the chest wall in early systole, producing the apex beat, normally no larger than one intercostal space.

blocks.caption: The base is the posterior surface, not the upper border. The right ventricle and left atrium form no PA contour because they are the most anterior and most posterior chambers, so they are judged on the lateral view.

blocks.text: A posteroanterior (PA) radiograph shows the heart edge only where it touches air-filled lung. The cardiothoracic ratio, the widest cardiac diameter divided by the widest internal thoracic diameter, is normally below 0.5 on a PA film in full inspiration. An anteroposterior (AP) portable film magnifies the heart because it lies farther from the detector, and a shallow breath raises the diaphragm and widens the shadow, so both can mimic enlargement.

Enlargement of one chamber changes the contour it forms. A dilated left ventricle, as in chronic mitral regurgitation, pushes the left border down and out and moves the apex beat lateral to the midclavicular line, often into the sixth intercostal space, raising the ratio above 0.5. Right atrial enlargement bulges the lower right border. Enlargement of the right ventricle and left atrium shows only indirectly (section C02).

sections.title: Front to back order of the chambers and its clinical consequences

blocks.text: From front to back the chambers lie in this order: right ventricle, then right atrium and left ventricle, then left atrium. The right ventricle sits directly behind the sternum and the left fourth and fifth costal cartilages. The left atrium is the most posterior chamber, separated from the esophagus only by the pericardium and the oblique pericardial sinus (section C03), with the descending aorta behind and to its left and the tracheal bifurcation and left main bronchus just above it.
The anterior right ventricle

A blade entering just left of the sternum meets the right ventricle first, so it is the chamber most often injured by penetrating trauma (section C06). When the right ventricle hypertrophies or dilates, as in pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary stenosis, its contraction lifts the left parasternal chest wall (a parasternal lift or heave), and on a lateral film it fills the clear space behind the lower sternum.
The posterior left atrium

The left atrium enlarges under a sustained pressure or volume load, classically mitral stenosis and chronic mitral regurgitation. It cannot expand forward past the ventricles, so it pushes backward and upward. It compresses the esophagus from the front, which causes dysphagia for solids and an indentation on the front of the barium-filled esophagus. It lifts the left main bronchus and widens the carinal angle. Together with the dilated pulmonary artery of secondary pulmonary hypertension, it can stretch the left recurrent laryngeal nerve under the aortic arch and cause hoarseness (section C04). On the PA film the enlarged left auricle straightens the left border below the pulmonary trunk, and the atrium itself projects to the right as a second curved edge, a double density.

blocks.title: How mitral stenosis produces symptoms outside the heart
steps: Narrowed mitral valve raises left atrial pressure
Left atrium dilates over months to years
Atrium can expand only backward and upward
Compressed esophagus causes dysphagia
Left main bronchus is lifted and the carina widens
Stretched left recurrent laryngeal nerve causes hoarseness
blocks.caption: The symptoms come from the neighbors of the left atrium. The same enlargement slows flow and favors atrial fibrillation and thrombus in the left auricle.

blocks.text: The same position is the basis of transesophageal echocardiography. A probe in the esophagus lies millimeters from the left atrium with no lung or chest wall between, so it images the left atrium and left auricle far better than a chest wall probe and is the preferred way to look for auricular thrombus.

blocks.title: Reasoning from symptoms to the left atrium
blocks.text: A 42-year-old woman with past rheumatic fever has exertional breathlessness, dysphagia for solids, and hoarseness. Her film shows a straight left heart border, a double density on the right, and an elevated left main bronchus. Step 1: the esophagus, left recurrent laryngeal nerve, and carina all lie behind or just above the left atrium, so the atrium is enlarged. Step 2: the straight border is the enlarged left auricle, and the double density is the atrium projecting right behind the right atrium. Step 3: rheumatic fever most often scars the mitral valve, and mitral stenosis raises left atrial pressure. Step 4: that pressure passes back through the pulmonary veins to the pulmonary capillaries and increases filtration, causing breathlessness. One lesion explains every finding through the position of the left atrium.

sections.title: Pericardium, pericardial sinuses, and referred pericardial pain

blocks.text: Fibrous and serous layers

The fibrous pericardium is a tough sac of dense connective tissue fused below to the central tendon of the diaphragm, blended above with the adventitia of the great vessels, and tied to the sternum by sternopericardial ligaments. It anchors the heart, moves it with the diaphragm, and is nearly inelastic over short periods, so it prevents sudden overdistension but also lets rapidly entering fluid compress the heart (section C06).

The serous pericardium is a closed sac of mesothelium (CV-2). Its parietal layer lines the fibrous sac and reflects around the great vessels to become the visceral layer, the epicardium. Between them lies the pericardial cavity, a potential space holding about 15 to 50 mL of serous fluid that lets the surfaces glide. Like a fist pushed into an underinflated balloon, the heart lies outside the cavity, covered by one wall of it.
Reflections and sinuses

The serous layer reflects in two separate sleeves: one around the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, the other around the venae cavae and pulmonary veins. Two recesses form between and behind them. The transverse sinus arises when the dorsal mesocardium breaks down during looping (CV-1); a finger passed through it isolates the great arteries from the venous side. The oblique sinus is a blind pouch behind the left atrium, closed above and at the sides by the venous reflection, and its back wall lies against the esophagus.

blocks.text: Blood supply, nerves, and referred pain

The pericardium is supplied mainly by the pericardiacophrenic arteries from the internal thoracic arteries, and the epicardium by the coronary arteries. The phrenic nerves (C3 to C5) descend between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura, in front of the lung roots, and carry pain from the fibrous and parietal layers; the visceral layer is largely insensitive. Vagal and sympathetic fibers also reach the pericardium but do not explain its characteristic pain. Because the supraclavicular nerves (C3 and C4) bring skin input from the shoulder to the same segments, pericarditis and diaphragmatic irritation refer pain to the trapezius ridge.

blocks.text: Ischemic myocardial pain differs because it travels with sympathetic afferents to about T1 to T5 and is felt as central chest pressure spreading to the medial left arm or jaw, with little change on breathing or posture. Pericardial pain is sharp, worse on deep inspiration and lying flat, and often eased by sitting forward. The inspiratory worsening reflects movement against the neighboring pleura; the postural effect is less certain. Inflamed serous surfaces rubbing together produce a scratchy friction rub with up to three components (atrial systole, ventricular systole, rapid filling).

sections.title: The great vessels and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve

blocks.text: The ascending aorta lies inside the pericardium, so a tear there causes tamponade (section C06), and the pulmonary trunk spirals around it, reflecting the spiral aorticopulmonary septum (CV-1). When a mediastinal tumor or nodes obstruct the superior vena cava (SVC), the face, neck, and arms swell and chest wall veins distend as collaterals reach the inferior vena cava.

blocks.text: The commonest arch variation is a shared origin of the brachiocephalic trunk and left common carotid. A less common but tested variation is an aberrant right subclavian artery that arises last from the arch and passes behind the esophagus; it can cause dysphagia, and on that side the laryngeal nerve does not recur.
The ligamentum arteriosum and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve

The fetal ductus arteriosus, from the distal left sixth arch artery, shunts right ventricular output from the left pulmonary artery to the aorta. It closes within a day or two of birth and fibroses into the ligamentum arteriosum, running from the origin of the left pulmonary artery to the underside of the arch just beyond the left subclavian origin. The aortic segment between these two points is the aortic isthmus, the site of most coarctations and most traumatic tears (section C06).

The left vagus crosses the arch behind the left phrenic nerve and gives off the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks under the arch behind the ligamentum and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. The right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery. Each supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles on its side except the cricothyroid, so injury paralyzes that vocal fold and causes a hoarse, breathy voice.

blocks.caption: The long intrathoracic course of the left nerve exposes it to disease of the aortic arch, left atrium, pulmonary artery, and left lung.

blocks.text: The left nerve passes through the aortopulmonary window between the arch and the left pulmonary artery. An arch aneurysm, lung cancer or nodes in the window, an enlarged left atrium with a dilated pulmonary artery (section C02), or ductus surgery can injure it.

blocks.predict: A 68-year-old smoker develops hoarseness, and imaging shows a mass in the space below the aortic arch and above the left pulmonary artery. Why would a similar mass on the right side at the same level be much less likely to cause hoarseness?
blocks.explain: The left nerve hooks under the arch at the ligamentum arteriosum and so passes through the aortopulmonary window, where the mass lies. The right nerve hooks under the right subclavian artery in the root of the neck, well above the arch, because the right sixth arch artery regressed.

sections.title: Internal features of the chambers and ventricular wall thickness

blocks.title: Internal features of the four chambers
rows: Crista terminalis, fossa ovalis, caval and coronary sinus openings
Moderator band, three papillary muscles, supraventricular crest
Two papillary muscles; mitral and aortic valves in fibrous continuity
blocks.caption: Smooth atrial walls come from absorbed venous structures and rough walls from the primitive atrium; smooth ventricular walls are outflow tracts.

blocks.text: Atria

The crista terminalis (sulcus terminalis outside) separates the smooth sinus venarum from the pectinate wall. The SA node lies at its upper end near the SVC, and the AV node lies in the septum just above the coronary sinus opening, which sits between the IVC opening and the tricuspid orifice (CV-7). The fossa ovalis floor is septum primum; its limbus is septum secundum.

In about one quarter of adults the septa never fuse, leaving a probe-patent foramen ovale, held shut by higher left atrial pressure until coughing, straining, or pulmonary hypertension reverses the gradient.

The left atrium is smooth because it incorporates the primitive pulmonary vein, which is why four veins open into it. Pectinate muscles are confined to the narrow, hooked left auricle, whose stagnant flow makes it the usual site of thrombus in atrial fibrillation.
Ventricles

The right ventricle has coarse trabeculae and three papillary muscles whose chordae reach adjacent edges of the tricuspid cusps. The valve moves passively; the papillary muscles tighten the chordae in systole so the cusps do not evert. The moderator band carries part of the right bundle branch to the distant anterior papillary muscle so it contracts on time.

blocks.name: conduction-pathway
blocks.caption: Conduction pathway: the right bundle branch continues through the moderator band to the anterior papillary muscle.

blocks.text: The left ventricle has finer trabeculae and two large papillary muscles, each sending chordae to both mitral cusps. The posteromedial muscle usually has a single arterial supply and ruptures more often after inferior infarction (CV-8). The anterior mitral cusp is in fibrous continuity with the aortic valve, and the tricuspid valve attaches slightly closer to the apex than the mitral.
Wall thickness and the law of Laplace

The left ventricular wall, about 8 to 12 mm, is two to three times thicker than the right, about 3 to 5 mm, because peak systolic pressure is about 120 versus 25 mmHg. By the law of Laplace, wall stress equals pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness, and stress is a main determinant of myocardial oxygen demand. A pressure load adds sarcomeres in parallel and thickens the wall (concentric hypertrophy), returning stress toward normal. A volume load adds sarcomeres in series and enlarges the cavity (eccentric hypertrophy), and the larger radius raises stress.

Both ventricles are equally thick at birth because the ductus exposes them to systemic pressure. After pulmonary resistance falls, the thin right wall handles volume easily but tolerates an acute pressure rise poorly, so a large pulmonary embolism can cause right ventricular failure.

blocks.predict: A patient with a deep vein thrombosis in the leg and a probe-patent foramen ovale has a pulmonary embolism, and an hour later develops weakness of one side of the body. Explain how a venous clot reached the brain.
blocks.explain: The embolism raises right heart pressures. When right atrial pressure exceeds left, the flap opens right to left, and another thrombus fragment can pass to the left heart and aorta, bypassing the lung filter, and lodge in a cerebral artery (paradoxical embolism).
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on the fossa ovalis and the probe-patent foramen ovale.

sections.title: Blunt and penetrating chest trauma to the heart and aorta

blocks.text: Blunt trauma injures by deceleration and compression, so it damages tethered or trapped structures. Penetrating trauma injures whatever lies on the track, so anterior structures suffer most.
Aortic tear at the isthmus

The heart and arch hang mobile from the great vessels, while intercostal arteries and pleura fix the descending aorta to the spine, so deceleration shear concentrates at the isthmus. Most full-thickness tears are fatal at the scene; survivors usually have a pseudoaneurysm contained by collagen-rich adventitia (CV-2), which can rupture without warning. The film shows a widened mediastinum, a blurred aortic knob, the trachea and nasogastric tube pushed right, a depressed left main bronchus, and sometimes a left apical cap; first and second rib fractures signal a large force. Because much mediastinal blood is venous, these signs only suggest the diagnosis, which rests on CT angiography.

blocks.text: Myocardial contusion and commotio cordis

A sternal blow bruises the right ventricle most often, releasing troponin and causing arrhythmias; sinus tachycardia is commonest, and right bundle branch block fits the anterior course of the right bundle and moderator band. A precordial blow on the upstroke of the T wave, the vulnerable period (CV-7), can trigger ventricular fibrillation without structural injury (commotio cordis).
Penetrating injury and tamponade

Stab wounds injure the right ventricle most often, then the left ventricle, right atrium, and left atrium. If the pericardial wound seals, blood collects in the sac (hemopericardium); if it stays open, blood drains into the pleura as hemothorax. Over minutes the fibrous sac is stiff and its pressure-volume curve turns steeply upward, so about 150 to 200 mL can cause tamponade, whereas a slow effusion can reach a liter with little pressure rise.

Rising pericardial pressure first compresses the low-pressure right chambers in diastole. Filling, stroke volume, and arterial pressure fall, venous pressure rises, diastolic pressures in all four chambers equalize, and fluid muffles the heart sounds (Beck triad), with reflex tachycardia. On inspiration, extra right ventricular filling can only push the septum left in the fixed sac, so left stroke volume and systolic pressure fall by more than 10 mmHg (pulsus paradoxus). The jugular y descent is blunted. Electrical alternans and low voltage belong to large effusions, and hypovolemia can leave the neck veins flat.

Ischemia weakens contraction and output falls further
blocks.caption: Unless the blood is removed, each turn lowers output further, ending in pulseless electrical activity.

integration.text: Embryology explains most of this anatomy. Looping rotates the right ventricle forward and the left atrium backward, which sets the radiograph borders, the chamber most often stabbed, and the chamber that compresses the esophagus. Breakdown of the dorsal mesocardium forms the transverse sinus, absorbed venous tissue smooths the atrial walls, unfused septa leave a patent foramen ovale, and persistence of the left sixth arch artery as the ductus explains both the course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and the isthmus as the site of coarctation and traumatic tears. Histology and physiology add the rest: collagen makes the fibrous pericardium stiff and the aortic adventitia briefly protective, and the law of Laplace and ventricular interdependence explain wall thickness and pulsus paradoxus.

Pathology supplies the causes: rheumatic mitral disease after group A streptococcal infection enlarges the left atrium; pericarditis follows coxsackievirus B, tuberculosis, uremia, autoimmune disease, or infarction; and lung cancer and nodes cause hoarseness and SVC obstruction. Anatomic reasoning has limits. Radiographs are two-dimensional and distorted by AP projection or a shallow breath, vessel branching varies, and classic signs such as the Beck triad are often incomplete, so a missing sign should not exclude a diagnosis the mechanism predicts.

summary: The heart lies in the middle mediastinum, two thirds left of midline, with its apex behind the left fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line.

The right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface, the left ventricle the apex and left border, the right atrium the right border, and the left atrium most of the base; on a PA film the left contour is aortic knob, pulmonary trunk, left auricle, and left ventricle.

The right ventricle is most anterior, so it is most often stabbed or bruised and lifts the parasternal wall when hypertrophied; the left atrium is most posterior, so its enlargement causes dysphagia, a widened carina, and hoarseness.

The inelastic fibrous pericardium and the serous parietal and visceral layers enclose a fluid-filled potential space; the transverse sinus lies behind the great arteries, and the oblique sinus is a blind pouch behind the left atrium.
Pericardial pain travels in the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) and is referred to the trapezius ridge because the supraclavicular nerves share those segments.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum, a sixth arch remnant, so arch, aortopulmonary window, and left atrial disease cause hoarseness.
The crista terminalis separates the smooth sinus venarum from pectinate muscle; the moderator band carries the right bundle branch; the left auricle is the usual site of thrombus.

The left ventricular wall is two to three times thicker than the right because it generates about five times the systolic pressure; by the law of Laplace, the thicker wall keeps wall stress near normal.
Deceleration tears the aorta at the isthmus, the junction of the mobile arch and fixed descending aorta, widening the mediastinum.
Rapid hemopericardium causes tamponade with small volumes because the pericardial pressure-volume curve is steep, producing the Beck triad, equalized diastolic pressures, and pulsus paradoxus.

verify: The normal volume of pericardial fluid is quoted from about 15 to 50 mL; some sources give 20 to 50 mL.
The volume of rapidly accumulated blood that causes tamponade (about 150 to 200 mL here) varies between sources from about 100 to 250 mL.
Normal ventricular wall thickness values (left about 8 to 12 mm, right about 3 to 5 mm) vary with measurement method and source; the ratio of two to three times follows Moore.
Prevalence of a probe-patent foramen ovale is given here as about one quarter of adults; published figures range from about 20% to 30%.
Statistics on blunt aortic injury (the proportion dying at the scene and the proportion of surviving tears at the isthmus) vary between trauma series and are therefore stated without percentages.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms and alternative names Ortner (cardiovocal) syndrome, Beck triad, commotio cordis, bovine arch, and arteria lusoria, or only the descriptive terms used here.
The radiographic threshold for a widened mediastinum is quoted differently (often about 8 cm on a supine AP film) and was deliberately left out; confirm whether NABNE tests a specific value.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: heart-surfaces (anterior view with chambers forming each border), cxr-silhouette (PA cardiac contours), pericardial-sinuses (posterior pericardium with arterial and venous reflections), and arch-rln (aortic arch branches with both recurrent laryngeal nerves).
Order of chamber involvement in penetrating cardiac trauma (right ventricle, left ventricle, right atrium, left atrium) follows the usual consensus; reported percentages differ between series.
